supplement.holds: No supplementary file or appendix is identified. The included end matter consists of references (pp. 15-16) and Figures 1-6 (pp. 17-21). No external location for the unreported SDs, test statistics, or analyzed counts is given.

paper_design_summary: An eight-week university English creative-writing project describes 60 first-year non-English majors assigned to AI-supported instruction or traditional instruction, with 30 per group; the same methods paragraph calls the design quasi-experimental and says students were randomly assigned from two natural classes (p. 7, sections 3.2-3.3). Students used ChatGPT and image generators for ideas, drafting, revision, and multimodal presentation; teacher-scored writing and Torrance-based creativity results are presented as pretest/posttest means without instructional-arm labels or analyzed student counts (pp. 8-12). A nested comparison of student-generated and AI-generated images analyzes 30 works, which is an output-source comparison rather than a reported randomized-arm contrast (p. 13, Table 5).

studies.label: Eight-week college English creative-writing instruction, including a nested image-output comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: Reported assignment of students to multimodal generative-AI instruction or traditional teaching. field_rct and unit=individual follow the explicit student-random-assignment sentence in ordinary coursework, provisionally. The same paragraph calls the design quasi-experimental and refers to two natural classes; it does not describe the randomization method or resolve individual versus intact-class allocation. Repeated pre/post measurement makes the measurement structure mixed.
assignment.quote: Using a quasi-experimental design, students are randomly assigned to an experimental group and a control group (30 each).
assignment.locator: p. 7, section 3.2, Research Subjects and Sampling; p. 15, section 6.3 confirms two classes at one university

arms.name: Experimental group
arms.description: Teacher-guided use of ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL?E for idea generation, content creation, language refinement, and visual expression; the methods report 30 assigned students (p. 7, section 3.2). No analyzed count is reported.

arms.name: Control group
arms.description: Traditional instruction, group brainstorming, independent drafting, and teacher feedback/correction; the methods report 30 assigned students (pp. 7-8, sections 3.2-3.3). No analyzed count is reported.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, attrition, completed-posttest count, or analyzed student denominator is reported. The methods describe/target 60 students at assignment; that number is not relabeled analyzed. Table 5 reports 30 works, which cannot establish a student count (p. 13).
participants.who: First-year non-English major university students in two natural classes at one university. Two English teachers are instructors/interviewees and one AI technical staff member supports the platform; they are not added to the student creative-output sample (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 15, section 6.3).
participants.quote: The study targets 60 first-year non-English major university students (divided into two natural classes).
participants.locator: p. 7, section 3.2 (assignment/sample description); p. 15, section 6.3 (single-university setting); pp. 11-13, Tables 2, 4, 5 (no analyzed student counts)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL?E; model versions not stated (p. 7, section 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Teacher-guided prompting for ideas, metaphors, outlines, narrative structures, draft generation, persona-based stylistic examples, error diagnosis, and revision; DALL?E/image tools turn students? keywords or completed paragraphs into illustrations. The intervention combines text interaction, refinement, and image generation rather than isolating one AI role (pp. 9-10, sections 4.2.1-4.2.5).

task.description: English poems, story segments, and prose on cultural narratives, ecological writing, and identity imagination, with text-image multimodal work, presentations, and peer review (pp. 8-10, sections 3.3 and 4.1-4.3). Pretest/posttest writing themes are identical (p. 11, section 5.1).
task.duration: Eight weeks, 16 sessions, two per week (p. 7, section 3.3). AI training and pretests in Weeks 1-2, three practice rounds in Weeks 3-6, final presentation in Week 7, and posttests in Week 8 (pp. 7-8, sections 3.3.1-3.3.4). No per-writing-task time limit is stated.

outcomes.name: Creativity composite
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Torrance/TTCT-based scoring of AI-assisted texts (p. 12, section 5.2.1); writing evaluations use dual teacher scoring cross-validated with Grammarly/ChatGPT scoring tools (p. 8, section 3.4). The rubric, scoring range, teacher aggregation, number of texts, and analyzed student denominator are not supplied for Table 4. The unit is the scored text; participant-level aggregation is not established. Table 4 supplies pretest/posttest means without identifying the instructional group and supplies no SD, SE, CI, test statistic, or p-value. with_ai/yes follows the explicit description of the scored texts as AI-assisted; whether these are the separate Week 8 posttests is unresolved, and AI withdrawal is never stated. The composite formula is not reported. The conclusion instead says creativity rose from 3.4 to 4.6 (out of 5), without explaining how these numbers relate to Table 4 (p. 14, section 6.1).
outcomes.delay: Assessed within the instructional project; evaluation phase is Week 8 (p. 8, section 3.3.4). No later follow-up or exact interval from production to scoring is reported.

outcomes.name: Overall writing performance
outcomes.measure_detail: Writing quality scored on a 10-point scale using the College English Writing Evaluation Standards (2020); pretest/posttest themes are identical (p. 11, sections 5.1 and 5.1.1). General writing evaluation uses dual teacher scoring cross-validated with AI tools (p. 8, section 3.4). These are quality scores, not overall creativity or across-person diversity. Table 2 reports only means and printed improvements; no SD, SE, CI, analyzed n, or inferential result is supplied. AI use in instruction is established, but permission to use AI while producing these specific test texts is not stated. Consequently question and ai_available_when_produced are null rather than assuming with_ai or after_ai. The conclusion separately claims an average writing score increase of 12.6% while referring to the control group; no matching arm-level result or explanation is given (p. 14, section 6.1).
outcomes.delay: Assessed within the instructional project; evaluation phase is Week 8 (p. 8, section 3.3.4). No later follow-up or exact interval from production to scoring is reported.

eligibility.reason: The explicit random-assignment claim is recorded, and the classroom design is provisionally coded field_rct, but the same paragraph calls it quasi-experimental and refers to two natural classes without resolving allocation (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 15, section 6.3). The methods describe 60 students and 30 per assignment group; the number analyzed across arms is never reported, so the required 50 analyzed people cannot be confirmed (p. 7, section 3.2; pp. 11-13, results tables). Output-scored creativity is explicit: Torrance dimensions are scored on AI-assisted texts and reported in Table 4, with dual teacher scoring described in the methods (p. 8, section 3.4; p. 12, section 5.2.1). Core eligibility therefore remains unclear. context_class=ai_vs_human applies only to the nested student-image versus AI-image comparison of 30 works in Table 5 (p. 13), not to the whole instructional study. No across-person diversity or explicitly AI-withdrawn outcome is established.

one_line_finding: The printed creativity composite rises from 5.5 pretest to 7.0 posttest (+27.3%; p. 12, Table 4), but the table gives no instructional-arm labels, analyzed student count, or statistical uncertainty.
open_questions: Was allocation genuinely randomized at the student level, randomized by class, or nonrandom intact-class allocation, given the conflicting wording in p. 7, section 3.2?
How many students were analyzed in each instructional arm and for each outcome, and were any assigned students excluded or lost before the posttests?
Do the pretest/posttest means in Tables 2 and 4 and Figure 1 represent the experimental group, both groups pooled, or another subset, and where are the control-group results?
Was AI permitted during the Week 8 writing and creativity posttests, and does Table 4 score those tests or the AI-assisted texts produced during practice?
What does the duplicated Syntactic Complexity label in Table 2 represent, and how do its writing improvement and Table 4 creativity scores relate to the different values in the conclusion?

How were the student-generated and AI-generated image pools produced and scored; are the 30 works paired or split between sources, how many students contributed them, and were student images independently produced without AI?
Are the SDs, paired t-tests, ANOVAs, and correlations described in section 3.5 available anywhere? No such results, data/code link, or supplementary file is identified in this PDF.
notes: Read the full 40,410-character markdown conversion, including its end matter; checked every PDF page and visually inspected the embedded Figures 1-6 and the main tables. PDF page numbers equal printed Page x/21 numbers. One instructional experiment is coded: qualitative cases and the nested image comparison are not additional independent participant studies. No reuse of another paper?s participants is stated; sample_overlap therefore remains empty. The participant country is not explicitly identified in the sampling description and is left null, rather than inferred from the author affiliation or policy/project context. Outcome inventory: Table 1 lists writing fluency/syntactic complexity/lexical diversity, TTCT fluency/flexibility/originality/elaboration, motivation/self-efficacy/achievement goals, language errors, AI-use logs, and interviews (p. 8). Table 2 reports grammar accuracy, two separately printed Syntactic Complexity rows, and overall writing average (p. 11). Table 4 reports the four creativity dimensions and their composite (p. 12). Table 5 reports imagery complexity, spatial layers, metaphor visibility, and cultural symbol density (p. 13). Figure 1 reports article, subject-verb agreement, tense, voice, and spelling error rates (p. 17); Figure 2 repeats four creativity dimensions, despite its AI collaboration frequency caption (p. 17). Figures 3-4 are illustrative images (pp. 18-19). Figure 5 visualizes the image dimensions, and Figure 6 reports motivation, satisfaction, and concerns (pp. 20-21). The main 15 output outcomes are listed, prioritizing creativity, the tabulated writing/image scores, and the two error types emphasized in the results prose. Because of the outcome cap, separate records for tense, voice, and spelling errors in Figure 1 are omitted. Also omitted as separate secondary outcomes are prose-only student-image element completeness, abstraction level, square-building/flower/light element proportions, AI-image conceptual transformation, and the illustrative spatial-depth description (p. 13, section 5.2.2); their coding and denominators are not supplied. Motivation, satisfaction, perceived creativity/language improvement, feedback timeliness, self-editing awareness, dependence concerns, usage logs, and interview themes are not output-scored creativity outcomes and are not entered (pp. 10-14; Figure 6). No actual collaboration-frequency statistics are recoverable from Figure 2: its plotted data concern creativity. Figure 5 pie shares are not interpreted as treatment effect sizes. No Table 3 occurs in this PDF. Table 2 genuinely duplicates the Syntactic Complexity label; this is not corrected from the surrounding mention of lexical diversity. Conflicting conclusion values are retained as discrepancies in the relevant measure details, not converted into additional effect estimates. The statistics_available label arm_means_sds_ns denotes available means in these entries only: it does not assert that SDs or analyzed people counts are available. No standardized effects are computed, and all printed changes/percentages are transcribed rather than recalculated. Before_after contrast names identify the printed timepoints, not the instructional arms, because the tables do not identify their underlying group. The field_rct design and randomized=yes record the paper?s explicit claim; eligibility separately flags its conflicting description. Null categorical fields are used where the form offers no unknown category and the source does not establish AI availability, the applicable timing question, or the image-scoring method. immediate denotes assessment within the teaching project, not an independently demonstrated zero-day delay.
